notes.text: At the pentecost of Sinai, in the Old Testament, and the pentecost of Jerusalem, in the New, where the two grand manifestations of God, the legal and the evangelical; the one from the mountain, and the other from heaven; the terrible, and the merciful one. They were all with one accord in one place — So here was a conjunction of company, minds, and place; the whole hundred and twenty being present.
And suddenly there came a sound from heaven — So will the Son of man come to judgment. And it filled all the house - That is, all that part of the temple where they were sitting.

And there appeared distinct tongues, as of fire — That is, small flames of fire. This is all which the phrase, tongues of fire, means in the language of the seventy. Yet it might intimate God's touching their tongues as it were (together with their hearts) with Divine fire: his giving them such words as were active and penetrating, even as flaming fire.

And they began to speak with other tongues — The miracle was not in the ears of the hearers, (as some have unaccountably supposed,) but in the mouth of the speakers. And this family praising God together, with the tongues of all the world, was an earnest that the whole world should in due time praise God in their various tongues. As the Spirit gave them utterance - Moses, the type of the law, was of a slow tongue; but the Gospel speaks with a fiery and flaming one.
And there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews — Gathered from all parts by the peculiar providence of God.
The multitude came together, and were confounded — The motions of their minds were swift and various.
Judea — The dialect of which greatly differed from that of Galilee. Asia - The country strictly so called.
Roman sojourners — Born at Rome, but now living at Jerusalem. These seem to have come to Jerusalem after those who are above mentioned. All of them were partly Jews by birth, and partly proselytes.

Cretans — One island seems to be mentioned for all. The wonderful works of God - Probably those which related to the miracles, death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ, together with the effusion of his Spirit, as a fulfilment of his promises, and the glorious dispensations of Gospel grace.
They were all amazed — All the devout men.

But others mocking — The world begins with mocking, thence proceeds to cavilling, chap. iv, 7; to threats, iv, 17; to imprisoning, chap. v, 18; blows, v, 40; to slaughter, chap. vii, 58. These mockers appear to have been some of the natives of Judea, and inhabitants of Jerusalem, (who understood only the dialect of the country,) by the apostle's immediately directing his discourse to them in the next verse. They are full of sweet wine - So the Greek word properly signifies. There was no new wine so early in the year as pentecost. Thus natural men are wont to ascribe supernatural things to mere natural causes; and many times as impudently and unskilfully as in the present case.

Then Peter standing up — All the gestures, all the words of Peter, show the utmost sobriety; lifted up his voice - With cheerfulness and boldness; and said to them - This discourse has three parts; each of which, ver. 14, 22, 29, begins with the same appellation, men: only to the last part he prefixes with more familiarity the additional word brethren. Men of Judea - That is, ye that are born in Judea. St. Peter spoke in Hebrew, which they all understood.
It is but the third hour of the day — That is, nine in the morning. And on the solemn festivals the Jews rarely ate or drank any thing till noon.
But this is that which was spoken of by the prophet — But there is another and better way of accounting for this. Joel ii, 28

The times of the Messiah are frequently called the last days, the Gospel being the last dispensation of Divine grace. I will pour out of my Spirit — Not on the day of pentecost only, upon all flesh - On persons of every age, sex, and rank. And your young men shall see visions - In young men the outward sense, are most vigourous, and the bodily strength is entire, whereby they are best qualified to sustain the shock which usually attends the visions of God. In old men the internal senses are most vigourous, suited to divine dreams. Not that the old are wholly excluded from the former, nor the young from the latter.
And upon my servants — On those who are literally in a state of servitude.

And I will show prodigies in heaven above, and signs on earth beneath — Great Revelations of grace are usually attended with great judgments on those who reject it. In heaven - Treated of, ver. 20. On earth - Described in this verse. Such signs were those mentioned, ver. 22, before the passion of Christ; which are so mentioned as to include also those at the very time of the passion and resurrection, at the destruction of Jerusalem, and at the end of the world. Terrible indeed were those prodigies in particular which preceded the destruction of Jerusalem: such as the flaming sword hanging over the city, and the fiery comet pointing down upon it for a year; the light that shone upon the temple and the altar in the night, as if it had been noon-day; the opening of the great and heavy gate of the temple without hands; the voice heard from the most holy place, Let us depart hence; the admonition of Jesus the son of Ananus, crying for seven years together, Woe, woe, woe; the vision of contending armies in the air, and of entrenchments thrown up against a city there represented; the terrible thunders and lightnings, and dreadful earthquakes, which every one considered as portending some great evil: all which, through the singular providence of God, are particularly recorded by Josephus. Blood - War and slaughter. Fire - Burnings of houses and towns, involving all in clouds of smoke.

The moon shall be turned into blood — A bloody colour: before the day of the Lord - Eminently the last day; though not excluding any other day or season, wherein the Lord shall manifest his glory, in taking vengeance of his adversaries.

But — whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord - This expression implies the whole of religion, and particularly prayer uttered in faith; shall be saved - From all those plagues; from sin and hell.

glossa.text: *In the same place.* Namely in the upper room, into which they had gone up. He who desires the Spirit treads upon the dwelling-place of the flesh, transcending it by the contemplation of the mind.

*From heaven.* The Spirit is given from heaven, that God may be loved; on earth he is given, that the neighbour may be loved: for twice after the resurrection was he given, for the commending of the two precepts of charity. *A sound.* It may be called the speaking of tongues sounding from the mouth of the apostles. *Spirit.* Before the passion the Spirit was given to the apostles for the grace of teaching and of healings; after the resurrection Jesus breathed the spirit, and said: *Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them ((Joan. XX))*, etc. Which gift he had given to Peter alone beforehand: but, as is believed, then by anticipation, now with the rest by completion it is bestowed on Peter also: and the power of forgiving was given to those whom he was sending to the office of preaching.

*Mighty.* By comparison with what went before, the grace of the apostles is called mighty, or the Spirit came in the likeness of a mighty wind. *The whole house.* The Spirit is poured into them sitting in one house, that the unity of the Church may be commended, the third law beginning in the upper room. At the giving of the law the people stood far off for fear; here, at the coming of the Spirit, they had been gathered into one out of love. *Sitting.* That there might be fulfilled what had been said to them: *Sit you here in the city.* Sitting is a token of humility and of stability: by which a seat is prepared for the Holy Spirit, who rests upon the humble.

 ((GREG.)) The Spirit appeared in fire, but through himself, etc., *as far as* and hearts were taught by the voice or by the sound.

*Parted.* The dispersion of tongues was made at the tower, but what pride dispersed, humility gathers together again: in pride is dispersion, in humility concord is made. Behold, the sentence of the Lord is fulfilled which says: *I will not leave you orphans, but I will send the Paraclete Spirit ((Joan. XIV))*, who, being their advocate, spoke for them in all tongues. He brought tongues, who came for the Word, for the tongue has kinship with the word, so that they cannot be separated from one another. So the Word of the Father, that is the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparable, nay rather of one nature. *As of fire.* The same Spirit came in fire: because sinners *the Spirit purges, enlightens, kindles, burns.* For fire has four natures, *it burns, purges, warms, enlightens.* In like manner the Spirit burns up sins, purges hearts, shakes off torpor, illumines ignorances. Fire is incorporeal and invisible in its own nature; but when some body has been assumed it is seen, appearing of diverse colour, on account of the materials in which it burns. So the Spirit will not be able to be seen, save through the creatures in which he works.

*And they began.* Behold the sign of fulness: a full vessel bursts out. Fire cannot be hidden in the bosom. *With divers tongues.* Because they spoke with all tongues, or, speaking in their own, that is the Hebrew tongue, they were so understood by all as if they spoke in the proper tongues of each, according to that of the Prophet: In other tongues and with other lips will I speak to this people, etc.
*Out of every nation,* etc. ((RAB.)) As if it were said: Wheresoever born. But the captivity, which was made under Antiochus not many times before, caused the Jews to be born among all nations.

*Confounded.* That confusion is set over against the confusion of tongues, from which Babel obtained its name. So the humility of the apostles answers to human pride. *Every man.* All the tongues are said to be seventy-two: whence also the disciples of the second order were chosen under this number, that the number of the preachers might accord with the number of the tongues.

*We have heard.* In this it was signified that one Church would speak in the tongues of all nations.

 ((BEDA.)) It is asked whether those who were speaking, etc., *as far as* it seemed rather to be a miracle of the hearers than of the speakers.

*Cappadocia,* etc. These five provinces which are set after Judaea do indeed speak Greek: but from the custom of their country there is a diversity in sound. Whence wonderful was the grace in the apostles, which not only taught them the diversity, but also made in their speech the distance of properties in each of the tongues according to the number of the provinces.
*Strangers of Rome.* In the Greek, sojourning Romans, that is, Jews who led a pilgrim life at Rome.
*Jewish men.* That is, there are two causes of prudence, namely that they were Jews, and that they dwelt in Jerusalem, which sobriety becomes.

*I will pour out.* By this word he shows the largeness of the gift, because the Spirit was to be given not, as of old, to prophets and priests only, but to all persons everywhere in either sex. *Of my Spirit.* He looks to the diverse gifts while he says this, but not to a diminution of the substance. *Upon all flesh.* What all flesh is he consequently expounds there: *And the sons shall prophesy,* etc.

((RAB.)) Upon all flesh, of male and female, or of the circumcised and the heathen, according to that: *There is not male and female, circumcision and uncircumcision, Barbarian and Scythian, bond and free ((Gal. III))*. 

*And they shall prophesy.* The law and the prophets until John: from him the kingdom is preached. But it is one thing to prophesy of Christ, another to foretell and to teach things to come.

*And I will give.* Mystically, wonders in heaven are labours in the Church. Signs, upon the earth. Vengeances, upon the earthly. Blood, in martyrdom. Fire, of the Gospel or of the Holy Spirit. Vapour of smoke, the compunction of the soul or of the heart. *Wonders in heaven.* For indeed at the birth of Christ a new star appeared; at his ascending the cross, the sun was darkened and heaven was overspread with darkness.

*Blood.* Not only of the wound, but also of the sweat, when in prayer his sweat became as drops of blood, which is set among the signs of the Deity, because it is not found in human nature. Therefore it signifies that the whole world is to be washed by the blood of Christ, that as the tabernacle had been consecrated by the blood of victims, so the faithful people might be dedicated by the blood of the same: and that not only at Jerusalem should there be a place of prayer, but that in every place of his dominion the elect should lift up their hands by prayers to the Lord. *Vapour of smoke.* A vapour, namely, of compunction and of weepings. Because as smoke from fire, so compunction from the ardour of the Holy Spirit.

*The sun shall be turned,* etc. This is believed to have been done partly in the passion of Christ, partly to be about to come before the day of judgment. For then the sun was darkened, but the moon turned into blood could not appear to men: because then (as being in the Pasch) standing as the fifteenth, it had by day been hidden from human sight by the interposing of the earth.

notes.text: Creeping — This word is common to all creatures that move without feet.

Leviathan — The whale. Therein - Who being of such a vast strength and absolute dominion in the sea, tumbles in it with great security, and sports himself with other creatures.

20. Darkness - Which succeeds the light by virtue of thy decree.
Hidest — Withdrawest the care of thy providence.

Spirit — That quickening power of God, by which he produces life in the creatures from time to time. For he speaks not here of the first creation, but of the continued production of living creatures. Created - Other living creatures are produced; the word created being taken in its largest sense for the production of things by second causes. Renewest - And thus by thy wise and wonderful providence thou preservest the succession of living creatures.

Rejoice — Thus God advances the glory of his wisdom and power and goodness, in upholding the works of his hands from generation to generation, and he takes pleasure in the preservation of his works, as also in his reflection upon these works of his providence.

He looketh — This is a farther illustration of God's powerful providence: as when he affords his favour to creatures, they live and thrive, so on the contrary, one angry look or touch of his upon the hills or earth, makes them tremble and smoke, as Sinai did when God appeared in it.

glossa.text: *With possession.* ((AUG.)) Elsewhere, *creature.* ((ID.)) Through Christ the Father, etc., *as far as* yet the wood was given, upon which we might sail across.

*This great sea,* etc. ((CASS.)) The second part, where he says: How he leads the Church across the sea of this world to the shore of the homeland. *Creeping things,* etc. ((AUG.)) Evil spirits, whose snares creep.

*This dragon which thou hast formed.* ((ID.)) Besides these animals, etc., *as far as* he was made greater in malice. *For mocking.* ((ID.)) It is said in Job *(Job XL)* that Satan is mocked by the angels of God, who are set over the powers of the air, that they may not hurt us.

*Meat.* ((ID.)) The dragon's food is earth, because it was said to him: *Thou shalt eat earth all the days of my life ((Gen. III))*. Because they that love earthly things are the devil's food. But the food of the just man is the word of God, whence, *Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God ((Deut. VIII))*.
*Thy hand, all things shall be filled with good.* ((CASS.)) Or the hand is the power which abundantly fills all things.

*But when thou turnest away.* ((AUG.)) Many, being filled with good, have ascribed it to themselves; but God, willing to prove to them that they have it not from themselves but from God, so that with the good they may have humility, sometimes troubles them, turns away his face, and they fall into temptation.
*Send forth thy spirit.* ((CASS.)) The dust is called theirs, because from themselves they have it that they are dust. But the Spirit is the Lord's: behold the medicine for those returned into dust.

*To tremble.* ((AUG.)) Better is the trembling of humility than the confidence of pride. Whence the Apostle: *With trembling work out your salvation ((Phil. II))*. *The mountains.* ((ID.)) Those who were proud, boasting that all things came from themselves. Even as it happened on mount Sina.

*I will sing.* ((CASS.)) The third part, where he promises that he will sing always. As if he should say: These foretold things the Lord has done, and these being beheld. *In my life.* ((AUG.)) Present and to come; of hope and of sight. Now hope is our life, afterwards it shall be eternal. The life of mortal life is the hope of immortal life. *As long as I am.* ((ID.)) Because in him I am without end, I will sing psalms as long as I am, lest any other act of that life be supposed than to sing psalms: because he who is praised cannot come to be wearisome, it does not become wearisome to praise him; but he is ever loved, ever praised.

*Let it be pleasant.* Another reading: *Let my disputation be sweet to him.* ((AUG.)) For the disputation of man with God is the confession of sins. Whence Isaiah ((Isa. I)). *Take away the wickednesses from your souls, say ye to do well, judge for the fatherless, and come and let us dispute, saith the Lord.* Thy disputation, therefore, is the sacrifice of thy humility, which is sweet to God.

notes.text: For the whole creation groaneth together — With joint groans, as it were with one voice. And travaileth - Literally, is in the pains of childbirth, to be delivered of the burden of the curse. Until now - To this very hour; and so on till the time of deliverance.

And even we, who have the first-fruits of the Spirit — That is, the Spirit, who is the first-fruits of our inheritance. The adoption - Persons who had been privately adopted among the Roman were often brought forth into the forum, and there publicly owned as their sons by those who adopted them. So at the general resurrection, when the body itself is redeemed from death, the sons of God shall be publicly owned by him in the great assembly of men and angels. The redemption of our body - From corruption to glory and immortality.
For we are saved by hope — Our salvation is now only in hope. We do not yet possess this full salvation.

Likewise the Spirit — Nay, not only the universe, not only the children of God, but the Spirit of God also himself, as it were, groaneth, while he helpeth our infirmities, or weaknesses. Our understandings are weak, particularly in the things of God our desires are weak; our prayers are weak. We know not - Many times. What we should pray for - Much less are we able to pray for it as we ought: but the Spirit maketh intercession for us - In our hearts, even as Christ does in heaven. With groanings - The matter of which is from ourselves, but the Spirit forms them; and they are frequently inexpressible, even by the faithful themselves.

But he who searcheth the hearts — Wherein the Spirit dwells and intercedes. Knoweth - Though man cannot utter it. What is the mind of the Spirit, for he maketh intercession for the saints - Who are near to God. According to God - According to his will, as is worthy of God. and acceptable to him.

glossa.text:
*Every creature. ((AUG.))* Man. Every creature is either corporeal, etc., *as far as* although not in all men. *Every creature. ((AMBR.))* All the elements fulfil their offices with labour, which is for our sake: whence they shall rest when we have been taken up; and therefore let us prepare ourselves diligently.

*It groaneth.* It is always new in this, which is marked by the inchoative verb, and for desire of the heavenly fatherland. *It travaileth.* That is, it grieves.

*Until now. ((AUG.))* Because although some one in Abraham's bosom has ceased to grieve, yet still in those who are not yet delivered every creature groans.

*Not only,* etc. ((AUG.)) That is, not only in the man of the body, but we also in our own selves apart from the body, the troubles of the body excepted.

*Not only. ((AUG., in expos. propos. in 53. in epist. ad Rom.))* Not only that which in men is called merely a creature, etc., *as far as* or with trouble disquieting.

 *The first-fruits of the spirit.* That is, of those whose spirits have already been offered to God as in sacrifice, and kindled with the divine fire of charity. *Adoption.* That the body also may receive the benefit of adoption, and that in every part they may be sons of God.

*For by hope.* He therefore says it that the merit of hope may seem the greater and therefore ought to save.

*The Spirit helpeth our infirmity. ((AUG.))* Because we groan and ask to be delivered, but lest we ask either before the time or contrariwise, the Spirit helps. What prayer obtains is evidently the gift of God, but to pray also is of grace.

*Unutterable.* For how should that be uttered which is desired, when it is unknown? Yet it is not altogether unknown. For if it were utterly unknown, it would not be desired. And again, if it were seen, it would not be sought with groanings.

*He searcheth. ((AMBR.))* Not as though seeking what he knows not, to whom nothing is hidden, and to whom the prayer of all spirits is known.

notes.text: When the Comforter is come, whom I will send from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me — The Spirit's coming, and being sent by our Lord from the Father, to testify of him, are personal characters, and plainly distinguish him from the Father and the Son; and his title as the Spirit of truth, together with his proceeding from the Father, can agree to none but a Divine person. And that he proceeds from the Son, as well as from the Father, may be fairly argued from his being called the Spirit of Christ, 1 Pet. i, 11; and from his being here said to be sent by Christ from the Father, as well as sent by the Father in his name.

glossa.text: *But when.* Now, seeing the works, they hate gratis both me and the Father. But when the Paraclete shall have come, he will convict by a more manifest testimony those who saw and hated; but some of them also, pricked for so great a crime, he will convert. *Whom I will send.* On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon a hundred and twenty men gathered together, with whom were all the apostles in the house where the supper had been. *Who from the Father.* The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, but the Son is said to proceed from the Father, because he is wont to refer to the Father even what is his own, from whom he himself is. From whom therefore he has that he is, from him he has that the Spirit proceeds from him.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Come, Holy Spirit.
Fill us with your fire and breath.
Like a rushing wind you filled the house.
And tongues of flame came down.
Send forth your Spirit, and we are created.
Renew the face of the earth.
Come, Holy Spirit. Come, let us worship.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Feel the air begin to move, a wind out of nowhere filling the whole house, until the room is loud with it.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!
See the fire come to rest on each of them, on the old and the young, the daughters and the sons.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!
When we have no words, only groans too deep for speech, the Spirit prays inside us and is heard.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!
Send your breath over these dry bones and this tired world, and make us new.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: A wind from heaven fills the house.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!
Flames come to rest on each of us.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!
When words fail, the Spirit prays in us.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!
Renew the face of the earth. Come, let us worship.
Come, Holy Spirit, come!
